title: Fed's Waller Signals More Rate Hikes as 10-Year Yield Nears 24-Year High
excerpt: The Fed governor left the door open for a pause at the October 27-28 meeting, but warned inflation remains more than a point above target as oil prices surge past $104.
body:
• Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said Thursday that additional interest-rate hikes will likely be needed to bring inflation back to the Fed's 2% target, but stressed there is "flexibility" about their timing.
  • The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.305% in late-morning trading, a day after touching a 24-year high of 5.37%; the 30-year yield held near 5.666% ahead of a $22 billion auction at 1 p.m. ET.
  • Waller, speaking at a Central Bank of Turkey forum in Istanbul, pointed to a strengthening economy, the unresolved energy-price shock from the Iran war, and fresh inflation pressure from the AI infrastructure buildout.
  • What it means for you: higher long-dated yields push up 30-year mortgage and auto-loan rates, tend to strengthen the dollar against the rupee, and make Indian equities and bonds less attractive to foreign investors chasing safer U.S. returns.

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said Thursday that the U.S. central bank will probably need to raise interest rates further to finish the job on inflation, but left the door open to skipping a move at the Fed's October 27-28 meeting — a signal that briefly steadied a bond market selling off for a second straight day.

Waller's message: hikes likely, timing flexible

Speaking from prepared remarks at a forum hosted by the Central Bank of Turkey in Istanbul, Waller was explicit about direction but deliberately vague about timing. "If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2% goal," he said. "But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."

He is the third top Fed official in recent days to signal a willingness to wait while leaving the door open to further tightening, according to Reuters. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has avoided giving much forward guidance since taking over, arguing that policymakers should not lock themselves in.

"With evidence that economic activity is strengthening in the second half of this year, I am not greatly concerned that tighter monetary policy threatens a damaging slowdown in the economy."

— Christopher Waller, Federal Reserve Governor

The context is straightforward: the Fed raised its policy rate by a quarter point in September, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, and the September projections showed most U.S. central bankers expecting another quarter-point increase before year-end. Investors now see the Fed holding steady at the October meeting — held a week before U.S. congressional elections — and raising rates at the December 8-9 session instead.

Bonds sell off for a second day

The bond market's reaction was swift. The benchmark 10-year yield rose 2.8 basis points to 5.305% in late-morning trading, after hitting a 24-year high in the previous session. The 30-year yield was flat to slightly higher at 5.666%, with an early-session reading of 5.705%, ahead of a $22 billion 30-year bond auction at 1 p.m. ET. The 2-year yield, which is the most sensitive to rate expectations, climbed 5.7 basis points to 4.821% after Waller's remarks.

Wednesday's 10-year note sale saw good demand across metrics, and analysts at J.P. Morgan expect Thursday's auction to go smoothly given fair valuations. "Continued outsized volatility in European sovereign debt markets relative to the U.S. provides near-term support from foreign demand," the bank's research note said.

Thursday's move was more orderly than earlier in the week, traders said. "There's some short-covering going on. The fact that there was good demand at the 10-year auction yesterday is a factor," said Tom di Galoma, managing director of global rates trading at Mischler Financial. Still, the yield curve flattened, with the closely watched 2s10s spread narrowing to 48.9 basis points from 51.4.

"The market remains content to trade the energy shock solely from the perspective of the inflationary implications, largely ignoring any potential demand destruction that could follow."

— Ian Lyngen, head of U.S. rates strategy, BMO

The oil and AI complications

Much of the pressure on yields is coming from the energy market. Brent crude jumped 4.7% to $104.87 a barrel, its highest in more than a week, while U.S. crude rose 4.6% to $92.30 — the highest since October 2 — on worries about oil supply following attacks on shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.

Waller named the energy-price shock from the Iran war, still unresolved, as one of his reasons for concern. His other reasons: a strengthening economy and new worries that the AI infrastructure buildout is adding to inflation by driving demand for key goods and services. Inflation remains more than a full percentage point above the Fed's 2% target, and the labor market has not cracked — weekly jobless claims came in at 197,000, below the 200,000 forecast.

Wall Street, meanwhile, has stalled after setting records earlier in the week. The Dow slipped 24 points to 51,156, the S&P 500 fell 19 to 7,782, and the Nasdaq dropped 158 to 27,381. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent downplayed the bond moves as a global phenomenon rather than a U.S.-specific one, even as the term premium in 10-year debt reached its highest in 12 years.

What comes next

The market's base case is now a hold at the October 27-28 meeting and a hike at the December 8-9 session, provided the data cooperate — low unemployment, continued growth, and limited progress on inflation. Anything that shifts that script — a weak 30-year auction, a hot inflation print, or commentary from Warsh — could send yields swinging again.

For Indian investors and NRIs, the implications are direct. A 10-year yield above 5.3% strengthens the dollar — the dollar index stood at 102.30 on Thursday — which pressures the rupee and raises the cost of imports. It also makes U.S. fixed income harder to compete with: foreign investors, who pulled thousands of crores from Indian stocks in late September, have less reason to chase emerging-market risk when Washington pays this much for safety. And for anyone borrowing, the pain is immediate — 30-year mortgage rates track the 10-year yield, and every basis point adds to monthly payments.
